text:
Indication for visceral surgical procedures should be based on clinical reasoning only and independent of financial incentives. Yet, there is a lack of studies investigating whether insurance type (basic vs. supplementary private) is associated with surgical procedure rates.

In this study we assessed whether incidence rates in adults with supplementary private insurance undergoing visceral surgical, non-emergency, in-patient procedures from 2012 to 2020 are higher compared to those with basic insurance only in Switzerland. We assessed incidence rates (IR) for basic only and supplementary private insurance stratified over time and by different age groups, and we fitted negative binomial regression models adjusted by inverse probability weights for specific visceral surgical procedures.

We used primary or secondary discharge procedure codes for one of the following procedures: cholecystectomy, fundoplication, sigmoidectomy, rectopexy, haemorrhoidectomy, inguinal, femoral, and umbilical hernia repair.

Of 1,954,119 surgical admissions (median age 63, 53.3% male, 15.3% non-Swiss nationality), 70.5% had basic insurance only. People with supplementary private insurance had a 7% higher probability (IRR, 1.07, 99% CI 1.06–1.07) to have a visceral surgical procedure done compared to people with basic insurance only—a result consistent across different types of procedures including cholecystectomy (IRR, 1.06, 99% CI 1.06–1.06), fundoplication (IRR, 1.09, 99% CI 1.09–1.10), sigmoidectomy (IRR, 1.10, 99% CI 1.10–1.10), rectopexy (IRR, 1.05, 99% CI 1.04–1.06), haemorrhoidectomy (IRR, 1.04, 99% CI 1.03–1.04), and hernia repair (IRR, 1.07, 99% CI 1.07–1.07). Sensitivity analyses, including side procedures, stratification by length of stay, and propensity score matching, suggested robustness of the results.

In this cohort study, supplementary private insurance was independently associated with a higher probability of undergoing a visceral surgical procedure. The role of financial incentives in surgical procedures is still unclear.

The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-026-28164-9 .

Since the 1990 s, health care spending generally outpaced economic growth in European countries. In 2020, European Union (EU) countries allocated an unprecedented 10.9% of their gross domestic product (GDP) to health care [ 1 ].Switzerland’s health care expenditure in 2020 was 11.8% of its GDP, placing Switzerland at the top in Europe [ 1 ].

A defining feature of the Swiss health care system is universal basic health insurance covering a fee-for-service model in outpatient care and case-based payments for in-patients according to the “Swiss Diagnosis Related Groups” (SwissDRG) system [ 2 , 3 ]. In addition to the universal basic insurance, residents can choose to obtain a supplementary private insurance, granting them additional benefits on top of the basic coverage [ 3 ]. These benefits include the ability to choose a physician in hospitals, two-bed rooms or single-bed rooms during hospitalisation, treatment in private clinics, and additional amenities (Supplementary eFigure 1) [ 3 , 4 ]. Whereas insurers have to accept every application for universal health coverage, applicants for supplementary private insurance need to fill out a health status questionnaire. In case of prior comorbidities, insurers are allowed to reject applicants for supplementary private insurance without explanation [ 3 ]. This presumably leads to healthier individuals being more likely to obtain a supplementary private insurance. It is widely speculated whether or not such a selection bias contributes to inefficient health care allocation. From basic insurance, providers receive a specific payment by SwissDRG, which is negotiated nationally on an annual basis [ 4 ]. Apart from this, separate contracts exist between providers and private health insurance plans covering benefits and services not included in SwissDRG [ 4 ]. In the past, physicians in public hospitals received sizable royalties for treating patients with supplementary private insurance in Switzerland.
